learningObjective: Distinguish peak (best-case) speedup from geometric-mean speedup and understand the scope-limits of reported paper numbers such as those in GSPMD.

canonicalClaims.claim: A paper's 'peak' speedup on a specific workload/hardware does not generalize to a geometric-mean across workloads: peak is the best-case observation and can be substantially higher than the geomean; when comparing systems, only comparably-defined summary statistics (e.g. geomean across a fixed benchmark suite) support fair conclusions.
conditions: The comparison spans multiple workloads with heterogeneous behavior.
The reported peak refers to a single (workload, hardware) pair.
nonImplications: Does not imply peak numbers are meaningless; they are useful to describe a system's best case, just not to summarize its typical performance.

canonicalClaims.claim: Reported speedups in a systems paper are conditioned on that paper's hardware, software stack, workload set and baseline; treating them as a general property of the technique overgeneralizes.
conditions: Baseline is stated (e.g. vs. manual placement, vs. a specific version of another framework).
nonImplications: Does not imply the technique offers no benefit outside the paper's setup; it means the specific numbers require restatement of conditions.

misconceptions.claim: If a paper reports a peak speedup of 2×, the geometric-mean speedup across models is also approximately 2×.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Peak is by definition the maximum observed value; geomean is a summary that is typically strictly smaller, often substantially so.

misconceptions.claim: A speedup reported vs. an older version of a competitor framework can be used as evidence against the current version of that framework.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Baselines evolve; comparisons must be against contemporaneous versions or explicitly qualified.

misconceptions.claim: Peak and geomean speedup are computed the same way and are interchangeable as summary metrics.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Peak = maximum; geomean = product-of-ratios^(1/N). They are distinct summaries with different sensitivity to outliers.
